newsitem.title: UK: Fashanu innocent of match-fixing, says lawyer.
newsitem.headline: Fashanu innocent of match-fixing, says lawyer.

text.p: The lawyer for former Wimbledon striker John Fashanu asked a jury on Monday to find his client not guilty of match-rigging, saying there was absolutely no evidence to convict him.
"I invite you to say there never was a case against John Fashanu and it hasn't been proved much in these proceedings," Trevor Burke told a court in the southern city of Winchester.
"I invite you as soon as you can to return the only proper verdict in this case and that is one of 'Not guilty'," he concluded in his summing up speech to the jury.
Burke said the prosecution had failed to prove its case that Fashanu was involved in attempts to fix matches for an Asian betting syndicate.
He said the striker was immensely wealthy in his own right and had married the daughter of a rich Ghanaian politician.
"The one critical factor in any charge of corruption is greed, the desire for money," he said. "Is this the kind of man who would be motivated by money?"

Fashanu and Malaysian businessman Heng Suan Lim are accused of passing cash from the betting syndicate to former Liverpool goalkeeper Bruce Grobbelaar and ex-Wimbledon keeper Hans Segers to fix matches by letting in goals.
Lim admits he paid the two goalkeepers to forecast the results of matches but all four deny rigging games. The jury is expected to start deliberating their verdict next Monday.

Bank statements showed Lim and Fashanu received huge sums of money from the Far East -- much of it from wealthy Indonesian cocoa trader and gambler Johannes Josef -- which the prosecution said neither man had been able to explain away.

But Burke said Fashanu and Josef were business partners, investing in a duty-free shop at Lagos airport and other ventures. Josef had sent Lim 150,000 pounds before the Malaysian met a single soccer player, he added.

The main evidence against Fashanu was supplied by chief prosecution witness Chris Vincent, who told the Sun tabloid newspaper that Grobbelaar had picked up 40,000 pounds at the striker's house for rigging a match.

Burke portrayed Vincent as unreliable and highlighted inconsistencies in his evidence. He also said it was sinister that virtually all the Sun's records of their dealings with Vincent had either been destroyed or had vanished.
"I suggest the Sun has destroyed the material because it showed just how inconsistent Vincent had been. It is little short, quite frankly, of a scandal," he said.
Burke said it was telling that Fashanu, unlike the two keepers, had not been accused of underperforming on the field.

"The Crown did not find a single incident worthy of you to consider by playing frame-by-frame film to show Fashanu missing an open goal, conceding a penalty or making a dreadful backpass which allowed the opposition to score a goal," he said.

Burke said the key to dismissing the charges against Fashanu was three games between Wimbledon and Liverpool in 28 days at the end of 1993, a time when the prosecution says the match- fixing gang was in full swing.
The Asian syndicates -- which won the largest amounts by betting on teams to either lose or win -- stood to pick up a fortune by ensuring Wimbledon lost, Burke said.

"Imagine the very best Christmas present for corrupt gamblers...you have three bent players in the same match. You could have Fashanu fluffing them up front and Segers dribbling them in at the back," he said.
The first game, a cup match, was drawn, and Wimbledon won the replay on penalties after another draw. The third match, a league game, also ended in a draw.
